current_answer: A new U.S. survey experiment found that a warning about students using AI instead of learning made hiring professionals rate recent graduates less favorably, especially high-GPA applicants. Those were hypothetical ratings, not interviews, hires or wages. A separate London field test found more interview invitations when some applicants signalled an AI-related certificate, but no job or pay outcome. Danish firm records still link reported AI adoption to slower hiring at some small firms; they do not establish AI-caused layoffs. Evidence for an individual worker remains limited by the population, stage and comparison each study actually measures.

catalogue_card.question: Can student AI use hurt a job application?
catalogue_card.text: A U.S. experiment found a warning about AI replacing student effort lowered hiring managers’ survey ratings. It did not measure real interviews or jobs.

summary: In a randomized U.S. survey, a strong warning about student AI use reduced hiring professionals’ ratings of hypothetical recent graduates, especially high-GPA applicants.
The study tested a belief frame, not actual employer decisions, completed hires or wages.

A London field test measured interview invitations from an AI-related credential, while Danish firm records link reported adoption to slower hiring at some small firms; neither predicts one worker’s prospects.
uncertainty: The new U.S. framing experiment measured stated responses to hypothetical resumes, not real hiring or pay.
Its Prolific sample is selected and cannot establish how common the tested beliefs are among employers.
The London credential experiment measures invitations, not completed hires, wages or the return from buying a course.
The Danish firm comparison is observational and its publisher abstract and author account report different growth-gap figures (11% versus roughly 9%).
freshness_note: Checked 10 October 2026. Added a U.S. survey experiment on employer ratings; real hiring and pay effects remain unmeasured.
